[[File:Solution of the Burgers equation - N wave.gif|thumb|300px|[[N-wave]] type solutions of the Burgers equation, starting from the initial condition <math>u(x,0)=e^{-(x-1)^2/2}-e^{-(x+1)^2/2}</math>.]]
'''Burgers' equation''' or '''Bateman–Burgers equation''' is a fundamental [[partial differential equation]] and [[convection–diffusion equation]]<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Misra |first1=Souren |last2=Raghurama Rao |first2=S. V. |last3=Bobba |first3=Manoj Kumar |date=2010-09-01 |title=Relaxation system based sub-grid scale modelling for large eddy simulation of Burgers' equation |url=https://doi.org/10.1080/10618562.2010.523518 |journal=[[International Journal of Computational Fluid Dynamics]]|volume=24 |issue=8 |pages=303–315 |doi=10.1080/10618562.2010.523518 |bibcode=2010IJCFD..24..303M |s2cid=123001189 |issn=1061-8562|url-access=subscription }}</ref> occurring in various areas of [[applied mathematics]], such as [[fluid mechanics]],<ref>It relates to the Navier–Stokes momentum equation with the pressure term removed {{Citation | url = https://www.uni-muenster.de/Physik.TP/archive/fileadmin/lehre/NumMethoden/WS0910/ScriptPDE/Burgers.pdf |title = Burgers Equation}}: here the variable is the [[flow speed]] ''y''=''u''</ref> [[nonlinear acoustics]],<ref>It arises from [[Westervelt equation]] with an assumption of strictly forward propagating waves and the use of a coordinate transformation to a retarded time frame: here the variable is the [[pressure]]</ref> [[gas dynamics]], [[traffic flow]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Musha |first1=Toshimitsu |last2=Higuchi |first2=Hideyo |date=1978-05-01 |title=Traffic Current Fluctuation and the Burgers Equation |url=https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1143/JJAP.17.811/meta |journal=Japanese Journal of Applied Physics |language=en |volume=17 |issue=5 |pages=811 |doi=10.1143/JJAP.17.811 |bibcode=1978JaJAP..17..811M |s2cid=121252757 |issn=1347-4065|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and [[mathematical physics]]. Burgers' equation also plays an important role in studies of the stability and dynamics of one-dimensional solitons with respect to nonlinear transverse perturbations of finite wavelength, since such perturbations are described by the [[Shrira-Pesenson equation]], which, in the single-wave approximation, reduces to Burgers' equation when the underlying soliton is stable.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Shrira |first1=V. I. |last2=Pesenson |first2=M. Z. |year=1984 |title=Soliton stability with respect to transverse perturbations of finite length and amplitude |journal=Nonlinear and Turbulent Processes in Physics |pages=1061 |bibcode=1984ntpp.proc.1061S}}</ref> '''Bateman-Burgers''' equation was first introduced by [[Harry Bateman]] in 1915<ref name="bateman">{{cite journal | author=Bateman, H.|date=1915|title=Some recent researches on the motion of fluids|journal=Monthly Weather Review|volume=43|issue=4|pages=163–170|doi=10.1175/1520-0493(1915)43<163:SRROTM>2.0.CO;2|bibcode=1915MWRv...43..163B |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>Whitham, G. B. (2011). Linear and nonlinear waves (Vol. 42). John Wiley & Sons.</ref> and later studied by [[Johannes Martinus Burgers]] in 1948.<ref>{{cite journal | author = Burgers, J. M.| title=A Mathematical Model Illustrating the Theory of Turbulence|journal= Advances in Applied Mechanics|volume=1|pages=171–199|doi=10.1016/S0065-2156(08)70100-5|date=1948| isbn=9780123745798}}</ref> For a given field <math>u(x,t)</math> and [[diffusion coefficient]] (or ''kinematic viscosity'', as in the original fluid mechanical context) <math>\nu</math>, the general form of Burgers' equation (also known as '''viscous Burgers' equation''') in one space dimension is the [[dissipative system]]:

:<math>\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} + u \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = \nu\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2}.</math>

The term <math>u\partial u/\partial x</math> can also be rewritten as <math>\partial(u^2/2)/\partial x</math>. When the diffusion term is absent (i.e. <math>\nu=0</math>), Burgers' equation becomes the '''inviscid Burgers' equation''':

:<math>\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} + u \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = 0,</math>

which is a prototype for [[conservation law|conservation equations]] that can develop discontinuities ([[shock wave]]s).

The reason for the formation of sharp gradients for small values of <math>\nu</math> becomes intuitively clear when one examines the left-hand side of the equation. The term <math>\partial/\partial t + u \partial/\partial x</math> is evidently a wave operator describing a wave propagating in the positive <math>x</math>-direction with a speed <math>u</math>. Since the wave speed is <math>u</math>, regions exhibiting large values of <math>u</math> will be propagated rightwards quicker than regions exhibiting smaller values of <math>u</math>; in other words, if <math>u</math> is decreasing in the <math>x</math>-direction, initially, then larger <math>u</math>'s that lie in the backside will catch up with smaller <math>u</math>'s on the front side. The role of the right-side diffusive term is essentially to stop the gradient becoming infinite.

== Inviscid Burgers' equation==

The inviscid Burgers' equation is a [[conservation law|conservation equation]], more generally a first order quasilinear [[hyperbolic equation]]. The solution to the equation and along with the initial condition

:<math>\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} + u \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = 0, \quad u(x,0) = f(x)</math>

can be constructed by the [[method of characteristics]]. Let <math>t</math> be the parameter characterising any given characteristics in the <math>x</math>-<math>t</math> plane, then the characteristic equations are given by

:<math>\frac{dx}{dt} = u, \quad \frac{du}{dt}=0.</math>

Integration of the second equation tells us that <math>u</math> is constant along the characteristic and integration of the first equation shows that the characteristics are straight lines, i.e.,

:<math>u=c, \quad x = ut + \xi </math>

where <math>\xi</math> is the point (or parameter) on the ''x''-axis (''t''&nbsp;=&nbsp;0) of the ''x''-''t'' plane from which the characteristic curve is drawn. Since <math>u</math> at <math>x</math>-axis is known from the [[initial condition]] and the fact that <math>u</math> is unchanged as we move along the characteristic emanating from each point <math>x=\xi</math>, we write <math>u=c=f(\xi)</math> on each characteristic. Therefore, the family of trajectories of characteristics parametrized by <math>\xi</math> is

:<math>x=f(\xi) t+ \xi.</math>

Thus, the solution is given by

:<math>u(x,t) = f(\xi) = f(x-ut), \quad \xi = x - f(\xi) t.</math>

This is an implicit relation that determines the solution of the inviscid Burgers' equation provided characteristics don't intersect. If the characteristics do intersect, then a classical solution to the PDE does not exist and leads to the formation of a [[shock wave]]. Whether characteristics can intersect or not depends on the initial condition. In fact, the ''breaking time'' before a shock wave can be formed is given by<ref>{{Cite book|last=Olver|first=Peter J.|url=https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-3-319-02099-0|title=Introduction to Partial Differential Equations|series=Undergraduate Texts in Mathematics | publisher=Springer| year=2013| isbn=978-3-319-02098-3|location=Online|pages=37|doi=10.1007/978-3-319-02099-0 |s2cid=220617008 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Cameron |first=Maria |date=February 29, 2024 |title=Notes on Burger's Equation |url=https://www.math.umd.edu/~mariakc/burgers.pdf |access-date=February 29, 2024 |website=University of Maryland Mathematics Department, Maria Cameron's personal website}}</ref>

:<math>t_b = \frac{-1}{\inf_x \left(f^\prime(x)\right)}.</math>

===Complete integral of the inviscid Burgers' equation===

The implicit solution described above containing an arbitrary function <math>f</math> is called the general integral. However, the inviscid Burgers' equation, being a [[first-order partial differential equation]], also has a [[First-order partial differential equation#general integral and complete integral|complete integral]] which contains two arbitrary constants (for the two independent variables).<ref>{{cite book |last=Forsyth |first=A. R. |author-link=Andrew Forsyth |year=1903 |title=A Treatise on Differential Equations |location=London |publisher=Macmillan }}</ref>{{Better source needed|reason=Might be better to source this statement with a book less than 120 years old.|date=November 2020}} [[Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar]] provided the complete integral in 1943,<ref>{{cite report |last=Chandrasekhar |first=S. |year=1943 |title=[[:s:On the Decay of Plane Shock Waves|On the decay of plane shock waves]] |id=Report No. 423 |publisher=Ballistic Research Laboratories }}</ref> which is given by

:<math>u(x,t) = \frac{ax+b}{at+1}.</math>

where <math>a</math> and <math>b</math> are arbitrary constants. The complete integral satisfies a linear initial condition, i.e., <math>f(x) = ax + b</math>. One can also construct the general integral using the above complete integral.

==Viscous Burgers' equation==

The viscous Burgers' equation can be converted to a [[linear equation]] by the [[Cole–Hopf transformation]],<ref>{{cite journal | first=Julian |last=Cole |author-link=Julian Cole |year=1951 |title=On a quasi-linear parabolic equation occurring in aerodynamics | journal=Quarterly of Applied Mathematics |volume=9 |issue=3 |pages=225–236 |doi=10.1090/qam/42889 |jstor=43633894 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | author=Eberhard Hopf|title=The partial differential equation u<sub>t</sub> + uu<sub>x</sub> = μu<sub>xx</sub> | journal=Communications on Pure and Applied Mathematics|date=September 1950|volume=3|issue=3|pages=201–230 | doi=10.1002/cpa.3160030302 | author-link = Eberhard Hopf}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Kevorkian |first=J. |title=Partial Differential Equations: Analytical Solution Techniques |location=Belmont |publisher=Wadsworth |year=1990 |isbn=0-534-12216-7 | pages=31–35 }}</ref>

:<math>u(x,t) = -2 \nu \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\ln \varphi(x,t),</math>

which turns it into the equation

:<math>2 \nu \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left[\frac{1}{\varphi}\left(\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial t}- \nu \frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial x^2}\right)\right]=0,</math>

which can be integrated with respect to <math>x</math> to obtain

:<math>\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial t}- \nu \frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial x^2}=\varphi \frac{df(t)}{dt},</math>

where <math>df/dt</math> is an arbitrary function of time. Introducing the transformation <math>\varphi\to \varphi e^f</math> (which does not affect the function <math>u(x,t)</math>), the required equation reduces to that of the [[heat equation]]<ref name="landau">Landau, L. D., & Lifshitz, E. M. (2013). Fluid mechanics: Landau And Lifshitz: course of theoretical physics, Volume 6 (Vol. 6). Elsevier. Page 352-354.</ref>

:<math>\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial t}= \nu \frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial x^2}.</math>

The diffusion equation [[Solving the heat equation using Fourier series|can be solved]]. That is, if <math>\varphi(x,0)=\varphi_0(x)</math>, then

:<math>\varphi(x,t) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi \nu t}}\int_{-\infty}^\infty \varphi_0(x') \exp \left[-\frac{(x-x')^2}{4\nu t}\right]dx'.</math>

The initial function <math>\varphi_0(x)</math> is related to the initial function <math>u(x,0)=f(x)</math> by

:<math>\ln \varphi_0(x) = - \frac{1}{2\nu}\int_0^x f(x') dx',</math>

where the lower limit is chosen arbitrarily. Inverting the Cole–Hopf transformation, we have

:<math>u(x,t)=-2\nu\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\ln\left\{\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi \nu t}}\int_{-\infty}^\infty \exp\left[-\frac{(x-x')^2}{4\nu t} - \frac{1}{2\nu}\int_0^{x'}f(x'')dx''\right]dx'\right\}</math>

which simplifies, by getting rid of the time-dependent prefactor in the argument of the [[logarithm]], to

:<math>u(x,t)=-2\nu\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\ln\left\{\int_{-\infty}^\infty \exp\left[-\frac{(x-x')^2}{4\nu t} - \frac{1}{2\nu}\int_0^{x'}f(x'')dx''\right]dx'\right\}.</math>

This solution is derived from the solution of the heat equation for <math>\varphi</math> that decays to zero as <math>x\to\pm\infty</math>; other solutions for <math>u</math> can be obtained starting from solutions of <math>\varphi</math> that satisfies different boundary conditions.

==Some explicit solutions of the viscous Burgers' equation==
Explicit expressions for the viscous Burgers' equation are available. Some of the physically relevant solutions are given below:<ref>Salih, A. "Burgers’ Equation." Indian Institute of Space Science and Technology, Thiruvananthapuram (2016).</ref>

===Steadily propagating traveling wave===
If <math>u(x,0)=f(x)</math> is such that <math>f(-\infty)=f^+</math> and <math>f(+\infty)=f^-</math> and <math>f'(x)<0</math>, then we have a traveling-wave solution (with a constant speed <math>c=(f^++f^-)/2</math>) given by

:<math>u(x,t) = c - \frac{f^+-f^-}{2}\tanh\left[\frac{f^+-f^-}{4\nu}(x-ct)\right].</math>

This solution, that was originally derived by [[Harry Bateman]] in 1915,{{r|bateman}} is used to describe the variation of pressure across a [[Becker–Morduchow–Libby solution#Taylor's solution: Weak shock waves|weak shock wave]]{{r|landau}}. When <math>f^+=2</math> and <math>f^-=0</math> this simplifies to

:<math>u(x,t)=\frac{2}{1+e^{\frac{x-t}{\nu}}}</math>

with <math>c=1</math>.

===Delta function as an initial condition===
If <math>u(x,0) = 2\nu \mathrm{Re} \delta(x)</math>, where <math>\mathrm{Re}</math> (say, the [[Reynolds number]]) is a constant, then we have<ref>Whitham, Gerald Beresford. Linear and nonlinear waves. John Wiley & Sons, 2011.</ref>

:<math>u(x,t)= \sqrt{\frac{\nu}{\pi t}} \left[\frac{(e^\mathrm{Re}-1)e^{-x^2/4\nu t}}{1 + (e^\mathrm{Re}-1) \mathrm{erfc}(x/\sqrt{4\nu t})/2}\right].</math>

In the limit <math>\mathrm{Re}\to 0</math>, the limiting behaviour is a diffusional spreading of a source and therefore is given by

:<math>u(x,t) = \frac{2\nu \mathrm{Re}}{\sqrt{4\pi \nu t}} \exp\left(-\frac{x^2}{4\nu t}\right).</math>

On the other hand, In the limit <math>\mathrm{Re}\to \infty</math>, the solution approaches that of the aforementioned Chandrasekhar's shock-wave solution of the inviscid Burgers' equation and is given by

:<math>u(x,t) = \begin{cases}\frac{x}{t}, \quad 0<x<\sqrt{2\nu \mathrm{Re}\,t},\\
0, \quad \text{otherwise}.\end{cases}</math>

The shock wave location and its speed are given by <math>x=\sqrt{2\nu \mathrm{Re}\, t}</math> and <math>\sqrt{\nu \mathrm{Re}/t}.</math>

===N-wave solution===
The [[N-wave]] solution comprises a compression wave followed by a [[rarefaction]] wave. A solution of this type is given by

:<math>u(x,t) = \frac{x}{t}\left[1 + \frac{1}{e^{\mathrm{Re}_0-1}}\sqrt{\frac{t}{t_0}}\exp\left(-\frac{\mathrm{Re}(t)x^2}{4\nu \mathrm{Re}_0 t}\right)\right]^{-1}</math>

where <math>\mathrm{Re}_0</math> may be regarded as an initial Reynolds number at time <math>t=t_0</math> and <math>\mathrm{Re}(t) = (1/2\nu) \int_0^\infty udx=\ln (1+\sqrt{\tau/t})</math> with <math>\tau = t_0 \sqrt{e^{\mathrm{Re}_0}-1}</math>, may be regarded as the time-varying Reynolds number.

==Other forms==

===Multi-dimensional Burgers' equation===
In two or more dimensions, the Burgers' equation becomes

:<math>\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} + u \cdot \nabla u = \nu \nabla^2 u.</math>

One can also extend the equation for the vector field <math>\mathbf u</math>, as in

:<math>\frac{\partial \mathbf u}{\partial t} + \mathbf u \cdot \nabla \mathbf u = \nu \nabla^2 \mathbf u.</math>

===Generalized Burgers' equation===

The generalized Burgers' equation extends the quasilinear convective to more generalized form, i.e.,

:<math>\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} + c(u) \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = \nu\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2}.</math>

where <math>c(u)</math> is any arbitrary function of u. The inviscid <math>\nu=0</math> equation is still a quasilinear hyperbolic equation for <math>c(u)>0</math> and its solution can be constructed using [[method of characteristics]] as before.<ref>Courant, R., & Hilbert, D. Methods of Mathematical Physics. Vol. II.</ref>

===Stochastic Burgers' equation===

Added space-time noise <math>\eta(x,t) = \dot W(x,t)</math>, where <math>W</math> is an <math>L^2(\mathbb R)</math> [[Wiener process]], forms a stochastic Burgers' equation<ref>{{cite journal |first1=W. |last1=Wang |first2=A. J. |last2=Roberts | title=Diffusion Approximation for Self-similarity of Stochastic Advection in Burgers' Equation |journal=Communications in Mathematical Physics |volume=333 |pages=1287–1316 |year=2015 |issue=3 |doi=10.1007/s00220-014-2117-7 |arxiv=1203.0463 |bibcode=2015CMaPh.333.1287W |s2cid=119650369 }}</ref>

:<math>\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} + u \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = \nu \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2}-\lambda\frac{\partial\eta}{\partial x}.</math>

This [[stochastic PDE]] is the one-dimensional version of [[Kardar–Parisi–Zhang equation]] in a field <math>h(x,t)</math> upon substituting <math>u(x,t)=-\lambda\partial h/\partial x</math>.
